title: Pfizer Stock 2025 Forecast: Will PFE Go Up Long Term? - The Globe and Mail
content:
Pfizer is looking to deleverage its balance sheet over the next few quarters, and expects to lower its leverage ratios to more comfortable levels. It also expects operating margins to gradually rise into the “mid- to high 30s.”

### Analysts Expect Pfizer Stock to Go Higher

PFE has received a consensus rating of “Moderate Buy” from analysts, and its mean target price of $36.11 is 33% higher than Wednesday’s closing price. Of the 18 analysts covering the stock, only 7 rate it as a “Strong Buy,” and 1 as a “Moderate Buy.” The remaining 10 analysts rate the stock as a “Hold.” [...] Moreover, even the most bearish of analysts covering Pfizer don’t see it dropping any further, as the Street-low target price of $27 is roughly flat with current prices. However, the Street-high target price of $54 implies the stock nearly doubling from these levels.

Amid the recent pullback, Pfizer stock has not only given up its COVID-era gains, but has retreated to levels last seen in 2016. While the decline in sales of its COVID-19 products has weighed on the shares, the stock’s risk-reward looks quite favorable at current levels - even as a rerating might take time, and could predominantly depend on how its product pipeline shapes up, especially after the obesity drug disappointment. Though this might bring investors little comfort, sector peer [Moderna](https://www.barchart.com/story/news/23927111/if-you-invested-10000-in-moderna-in-2019-this-is-how-much-you-would-have-today)[(MRNA)](https://www.barchart.com/quotes/MRNA) – which also developed a COVID-19 vaccine – hasn’t fared any better, and its 2023 drawdown was similar to that of PFE.

Will Pfizer stock go up over the next couple of years, or will the pharma giant's shares remain dead money? Here’s the 2025 forecast for PFE, and the key catalysts that could drive a rally in the stock.

### Why Has Pfizer Stock Fallen?

The key reason Pfizer stock has fallen over the last couple of years is due to dwindling sales of its COVID-19 products. That includes both the [COVID-19 vaccine Comirnaty and the Paxlovid pill](https://www.barchart.com/story/news/22752966/pfizer-from-pandemic-hero-to-investor-jitters) used to treat active infections.

title: The Pfizer Pivot: A Deep-Dive into PFE’s 2025 Financial Recovery and Strategic Rebirth
content: the peak of the COVID-19 crisis, the pharmaceutical giant is currently navigating one of the most challenging chapters in its 176-year history. With a stock price that has struggled to reclaim its former glory and a pipeline undergoing a massive strategic pivot, the Pfizer of late 2025 is a company defined by high-stakes acquisitions and aggressive cost-cutting. Historical Background Founded in 1849 by cousins Charles Pfizer and Charles Erhart in Brooklyn, New York, Pfizer began as a manufacturer of fine chemicals. Its early success was rooted in santonin, an antiparasitic, followed by a major expansion into citric acid production. The company’s trajectory changed forever during World War II when it became a pioneer in the mass production of penicillin, saving countless lives and [...] Management recently revised its 2025 revenue outlook to approximately $62 billion, the lower end of its previous range. Adjusted diluted EPS is expected to land between $3.00 and $3.15.  Cost Management: Pfizer is on track to achieve $4.5 billion in net cost savings by the end of 2025, with an expanded goal of $7.7 billion by 2027.  Debt and Cash Flow: The company carries significant debt from the Seagen acquisition, but robust cash flows from its legacy portfolio continue to fund the dividend and R&D.  Valuation: Trading at roughly 8x forward earnings, Pfizer appears "cheap" by historical standards, but the market is pricing in the "patent cliff" risks looming later this decade.
